clinicalPearls: A disorder of defective mineralisation of growing bone, most commonly due to deficiency of vitamin D and/or dietary calcium.
Risk factors include exclusive breastfeeding without vitamin D supplementation, darker skin pigmentation, limited sun exposure, and prematurity.

Skeletal signs include widening of the wrists and ankles, a rachitic rosary at the costochondral junctions, frontal bossing, delayed fontanelle closure, and bowing of the legs once weight-bearing begins.
Non-skeletal features can include delayed motor milestones, hypotonia, growth faltering, and increased susceptibility to fractures.
Severe hypocalcaemia may present with tetany, carpopedal spasm, or seizures, especially in infants.
Biochemistry classically shows low or low-normal calcium and phosphate, elevated alkaline phosphatase, raised parathyroid hormone, and low 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
Radiographs of the wrist or knee reveal metaphyseal cupping, fraying, and widening of the growth plate.
Treatment replaces vitamin D and ensures adequate dietary calcium, with biochemical and radiological healing confirming response.
Prevention through routine vitamin D supplementation in infancy is highly effective, and failure to respond should prompt evaluation for inherited or renal forms.
reference.pathophysiology: Vitamin D deficiency reduces intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate, lowering their availability for bone mineralisation. The falling calcium stimulates parathyroid hormone secretion (secondary hyperparathyroidism), which mobilises calcium from bone and promotes renal phosphate wasting. The combination of low calcium-phosphate product and PTH-driven bone resorption leaves the expanding cartilage of the growth plate and newly formed osteoid unmineralised, producing the soft, deformable bones and characteristic metaphyseal changes of rickets.
additionalDifferentials: Renal osteodystrophy from chronic kidney disease
additionalInvestigations: Serum calcium, phosphate, and alkaline phosphatase
Renal function and, where indicated, urine calcium and phosphate
Wrist or knee radiographs for metaphyseal changes
1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D in atypical or treatment-resistant cases
redFlags: Cardiomyopathy associated with severe hypocalcaemia or vitamin D deficiency
Failure to respond to appropriate vitamin D and calcium therapy
Progressive deformity or signs suggesting an inherited or renal cause
reference.prognosis: With adequate treatment, biochemical recovery occurs within weeks and radiographic healing over months; most deformities remodel in young children, though severe or late-treated cases may leave residual bowing.
pitfalls: Attributing bowed legs solely to physiologic causes and missing biochemical rickets
Overlooking dietary calcium deficiency as a cause even when vitamin D is adequate
Failing to investigate inherited or renal rickets when there is no response to treatment
Not providing routine vitamin D supplementation to exclusively breastfed infants
management: Replacement with vitamin D, as cholecalciferol or ergocalciferol, to restore bone mineralisation
Adequate dietary or supplemental calcium alongside vitamin D, as deficiency of either contributes
Urgent correction of symptomatic hypocalcaemia with calcium for tetany, carpopedal spasm or seizures
Preventive advice on sunlight exposure and diet, with routine vitamin D supplementation of at-risk breastfed infants
Monitoring of calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, parathyroid hormone and 25-hydroxyvitamin D, with radiographic confirmation of healing
Orthopaedic referral for residual limb deformity that fails to remodel
Investigation for inherited or renal causes if there is no response to adequate replacement
